contexts.context: The excerpt identifies ISO 10218-2 as the principal safety standard for robot system integrators, while ISO 10218-1 addresses robot manufacturers; both may be needed because some requirements appear in only one part. ISO 12100 provides the design and risk-assessment process, and IEC/TS 62046 and other device-specific B-type standards support selection and application of protective measures. For a robot-cell verification and commissioning file, the documented process should include risk assessment, identification of applicable safety requirements and directives, design against the Machinery Directive’s essential health and safety requirements, operating and maintenance manuals, and a maintained technical file. The responsible manufacturer or integrator must ensure that required documentation and tasks are completed, draw up the Declaration of Conformity, and apply CE marking. The excerpt’s example verification topics include guarding rotating parts and sharp hazards, maintaining adequate clearances, protecting against radiation, heat, debris and flying objects, selecting an appropriate operating mode before entry, verifying reduced speed below 250 mm/s where specified, checking hold-to-run and enabling devices, detecting personnel entry, and confirming protective or safety-rated monitored stops. It does not provide a complete commissioning test checklist or detailed collaborative-robot validation protocol, so those requirements should be obtained from the full ISO 10218-2 text and applicable functional-safety standards.

contexts.context: The excerpt frames robot-cell verification as part of a documented safety and risk-reduction process. The assessment should begin by defining machinery limits, including intended use, operating modes, training requirements, exposure, spatial and temporal limits, and environmental conditions. It then requires systematic hazard identification, risk estimation based on severity and probability, risk evaluation, and risk reduction. The document specifically recommends using checklists from ISO 10218-1 and ISO 10218-2, supplemented where necessary by ISO 12100. Risk-reduction measures should follow the priority of inherently safe design, safeguarding, and finally warnings or guidelines; information must not substitute for design or safeguarding. Before completion, risks and associated safety measures are to be validated to confirm that risks have been adequately minimized and residual risks are acceptable. For documentation, the designer’s process includes recording safety requirements and applicable directives, designing according to Machinery Directive Annex I, preparing operating, construction, maintenance, and safety manuals, compiling and maintaining a technical file, preparing the declaration of conformity, and applying CE and other required markings. The excerpt does not provide a detailed commissioning test checklist or specific collaborative-robot test procedures, but it identifies the standards and validation/documentation activities that should inform such verification.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a framework relevant to a self-driving laboratory safety risk assessment checklist, particularly for unattended robotic operation. Safety should be defined through an Operational Design Domain (ODD) containing equipment limits, chemical compatibility requirements, robotic exclusion zones, environmental conditions, and procedural sequencing dependencies. A safety envelope and multiple concurrent constraints should be used to ensure that thermal, pressure, collision, and other limits are satisfied simultaneously. During operation, Control Barrier Functions can filter AI commands through a real-time quadratic-program controller, using continuous sensor feedback to maintain forward invariance of the safe set and apply only the minimum correction needed to prevent hazardous actions. The architecture places safety enforcement in an orchestration and safety-kernel layer, with explicit safety gates between planning and physical execution. The CRUTD transactional protocol requires requests to be created, resources read and locked, actions simulated in a digital twin, tested against ODD and safe-set constraints, physically executed with continuous monitoring, and confirmed through state verification. Failures should cause an abort, rollback, and comprehensive logging. These mechanisms support verification of safety functions and incident traceability, but the excerpt does not specify emergency-stop test procedures, interlock test methods, responsible personnel, or a periodic re-verification schedule.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a safety assessment checklist centered on verified safety functions, bounded autonomy, monitoring, and escalation. Safety-critical components to assess include the Safety Kernel decision logic, control-barrier-function implementations, and emergency shutdown sequences. Safety requirements should be expressed precisely, including temporal requirements such as stopping within a specified time after obstacle detection, and model checking should exhaustively test all modeled input sequences. Verification artifacts, including counterexamples and identified invariants, should be retained to expose edge cases, boundary conditions, and undocumented assumptions. For unattended robot operation, autonomy should remain within a strictly defined operational design domain, with human standby or periodic oversight appropriate to the autonomy level, automatic escalation for boundary or novel situations, and clear anomaly-focused interfaces. Digital-twin predictions should be reconciled continuously with physical observations; unexplained divergence should trigger diagnostics and potentially restrict operations. Emergency-stop and interlock-related functions should therefore be tested as safety-critical functions and re-verified after incidents, constraint violations, corrective changes, or evidence of model or sensor degradation. The excerpt does not specify a fixed periodic re-verification schedule. Instead, it recommends competence-based progression, requiring substantial incident-free operational history before increasing autonomy, and automatic regression followed by root-cause analysis and corrective-action verification when safety performance deteriorates.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a high-level safety risk-assessment checklist for self-driving laboratories, but it does not provide a detailed checklist or specific procedures for unattended operation, emergency-stop verification, safety-interlock testing, verification of individual safety functions, or a periodic re-verification schedule. The proposed approach is an iterative six-step process: define the system, identify hazards, analyze scenarios, estimate risks, reduce risks, and validate the resulting safeguards. Assessment should account for heterogeneous fixed and mobile robots, chemical hazards, human–robot interaction, dynamic workflows, spills or unintended reactions caused by disrupted sequences, collisions with personnel or equipment, electrical hazards, chemical exposure, and maintenance-related ergonomic risks. The excerpt identifies perimeter safeguards, speed and separation monitoring, sensor-based human detection, dynamic safety zones, and operational-mode control as relevant mitigation measures. It also emphasizes that collaborative robots cannot be presumed safe and require rigorous, context-specific validation, including realistic force and pressure assessment where applicable. Therefore, the passage can inform checklist categories and validation principles, but additional source material would be needed to establish test steps, acceptance criteria, unattended-operation controls, emergency-stop and interlock verification methods, responsible personnel, and recurring review intervals.

snippets: The framework combines established robotics safety standards with laboratory-specific considerations, including chemical hazards, human–robot interaction, and dynamic workflows.
The proposed framework follows a six-step iterative process encompassing system definition, hazard identification, scenario analysis, risk estimation, risk reduction, and validation.
Risk mitigation strategies based on dynamic safety zoning, sensor-based human detection, and operational mode control were implemented to ensure compliance with safety requirements.

The results highlight the need for systematic, context-specific safety assessments in autonomous laboratories and demonstrate that collaborative robots are not inherently safe without rigorous validation.

the implementation of risk assessment frameworks and safety mitigation strategies, such as the establishment of robust perimeter safeguards, the incorporation of speed and separation monitoring mechanisms, the integration of sensor-based human detection systems, and the delineation of dynamic safety zones

contexts.context: The excerpt supports several elements of a self-driving laboratory safety risk assessment checklist. It describes a shared safety zone for multiple robots operating near laboratory personnel, with boundaries clearly marked and protected by safety laser scanners. Personnel intrusion triggers a two-stage response: an alarm and reduced robot speed, followed by a complete stop if the intrusion continues. Robot restart is restricted to authorized personnel and requires verification that the safety zone is clear; manual safety control units are used for reactivation. The system also includes a control function allowing authorized personnel to place robots in a safe mode during maintenance and development. These measures are relevant to verification of safety functions, emergency-stop or protective-stop behavior, access-control logic, and maintenance isolation. The excerpt emphasizes that safety assessment must cover the complete robotic system—including robot, end-effector, environment, and operational context—rather than relying solely on robot-level compliance. It also recommends conservative risk estimation and involvement of experienced operators, domain experts, and independent safety specialists. However, it does not specify unattended-operation procedures, formal emergency-stop verification tests, safety-interlock test methods, documented acceptance criteria, or a periodic re-verification schedule. The stated limitation that occurrence estimates may require longer observation periods suggests that ongoing monitoring and reassessment may be appropriate, but no interval is provided.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides several elements relevant to a self-driving laboratory robot safety risk-assessment checklist. Identified hazards included mechanical collision from personnel entering a moving robot’s workspace and chemical spills caused by dropped or improperly handled sample plates. The assessment classified exposure, occurrence, avoidance, and severity using a risk graph; robot collisions were classified as severe because pressure limits were exceeded, and one hazard produced a Risk Index of 5, above the action threshold of 3. Risk reduction focused on preventing robot motion when people entered the workspace. Safety laser scanners were implemented and validated to detect personnel and trigger an immediate stop. The safety-zone dimensions were checked against ISO 13857:2020 minimum separation distances. Robot safety functions were also tested by moving the end-effector toward a sensor until the built-in functions stopped motion, with repeated measurements performed under the most restrictive manufacturer settings. Additional safeguards included sensing systems and sealed plate covers for sample handling. The excerpt supports verification of safety functions, protective-device response, stop behavior, and separation distances. However, it does not specify unattended-operation procedures, emergency-stop button testing, interlock testing, or a periodic re-verification schedule. It only describes post-implementation validation and repeated collision measurement trials.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an interlaboratory collision-test campaign involving four TCP measurement positions, three movement directions, multiple velocity settings, and three body locations, producing 1,456 tests in total. It does not specify the number of repeated trials per individual condition. Impact force and pressure were recorded using a body sensor, while the robot controller exposed joint positions, velocities, currents, TCP forces, Cartesian pose, and tool speed. The excerpt identifies the robot as the expected principal source of variability, with differences potentially arising from robot model/version, controller, hardware structure, and brake reaction time; UR10 and UR10e systems were compared. Experimental setups also differed among institutes in controller, spring and damper materials, and sensor fixtures, including industrial robots with 60 kg or 165 kg payloads, an aluminium profile, and a welding table. Force generally increased linearly with velocity but included a nonzero force offset, rather than following the proportional relationship predicted by the simple ISO/TS 15066 inelastic model. The available passage does not give numerical force differences between laboratories or explain a detailed pressure-measurement calculation. For stiffness and threshold context, force-curve values used a nominal spring rate of 75 N/mm and were assessed against the hand threshold of 280 N.

For the final pendulum test, each setting was repeated five times and the mean was calculated. The study compared three force-measuring devices, while concealing their manufacturers. The excerpt does not describe an interlaboratory design, identify the number of laboratories, or report variability between labs. It also does not provide numerical force differences between laboratories. The devices were tested with different compliant elements and tappet geometries; the same spherical tappet had a radius of 25 mm, and a flat tappet had a diameter of 50 mm. The excerpt does not explain a pressure-measurement method or specify body-region stiffness settings. It does report stiffness-related test configurations: SH70A, SH30A, and SH10A materials for CC1, and 40 N/mm or 75 N/mm springs for CC2. Device flywheel masses ranged from a few hundred grams to 2 kg, with device 1 approximately 1.5 kg.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an experimental comparison protocol for force-measuring devices used in collaborative-robotics impact testing, rather than a complete interlaboratory comparison of PFL collision tests. For the pendulum tests, each setting was repeated five times and the mean value was calculated. The measuring instruments are force-pressure measurement devices incorporating mechanical compression elements (CC1 and CC2); their stiffness characteristics and the mass of moving parts were considered relevant. Dynamic testing used a test machine with a 200 N static reference point and a 10 mm starting distance, while different velocities were used to compare peak forces and oscillation behavior. The pendulum applied nominal energy levels of 0.5 J and 1 J, with actual values deviating by up to 5%. The study aimed to identify comparability and measurement uncertainty, but this excerpt does not provide numerical variability between laboratories or quantified force differences among laboratories. Pressure measurement methodology is not specified in the supplied text beyond the use of force-pressure measurement devices and different tappet geometries. Body-region-specific stiffness settings are also not explicitly reported; the excerpt instead discusses CC1/CC2 stiffness, spherical versus flat tappets, and pendulum energy levels. It notes that the lower energy level was selected because many hand-and-arm applications can operate up to that level.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that measurements were repeated three times only at the highest available robot velocity for body location 25, the back of the hand. At each sensor position (M1–M4), three movements were performed along the x, y, and z axes, producing 12 tests per velocity setting. The measuring instrument was a force/impact sensor incorporating an internal spring and damper; the highlighted test configuration used a 75 N/mm spring and SH70 damper, with impact forces evaluated against the ISO/TS 15066:2016 limit of 280 N. Five setup types were compared across laboratories. Force results generally showed similar trends, and spring constant and fixture type had limited influence in most configurations, although variability increased in sensitive configurations—especially ID5—and depended on impact direction, robot geometry, distance from the robot base, and fixture stiffness. The system stiffness comprised sensor spring stiffness plus fixture stiffness; fixtures ranged from a 60 kg-payload industrial robot to a welding table. Pressure measurement was not described as a specific standardized method in this excerpt. contexts.context: The excerpt reports comparisons among three biofidelic force-measuring devices, identified as devices 1, 2, and 3, using a test machine and a pendulum test bench. For device 1 at Q-point 1 and loading condition ID43, 30 repeated measurements were taken; the maximum-force standard deviation was below 1%. Average percentage standard deviations were 1.4% for device 1, 0.4% for device 2, and 0.6% for device 3, indicating greater stability for devices 2 and 3. Under identical settings, comparative peak-force differences between the three instruments reached up to 10%; a robot pre-study produced a 5% difference under identical conditions. contexts.context: The excerpt describes an interlaboratory comparison involving four European research centers: CNR, Fraunhofer IFF, DTI, and CEA. The test configuration was broadly standardized: all laboratories used the same UR10(e) robot family, standardized motion programs, contact scenarios, body locations, and measurement approach. However, robot controller characteristics and sensor fixture design were not prescribed and were treated as sources of between-laboratory variability. The biofidelic measuring instrument modeled a human body part as a mass-spring-damper system. Laboratories used either GTE Kolrobot 300N or GTE CBSF-75 Basic force sensors, together with TekScan I-Scan or FUJI foil pressure instrumentation. Tests considered sternum (location 8), abdomen (location 10), and back of hand (location 25). The corresponding spring stiffness settings were 25 N/mm for sternum, 10 N/mm for abdomen, and 75 N/mm for hand; damper hardness was SH70 for sternum and hand and SH10 for abdomen. Force evaluation used the highest peak in each force signal and compared it with the applicable transient-contact threshold. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide numerical stopping times or stopping distances for specific collaborative robots such as the UR10, UR5, or Franka Emika, nor does it describe a standardized measurement procedure for those robots. It emphasizes that stopping distance is safety-critical: a robot may continue moving after a protective stop or after exceeding a speed limit or virtual safety fence, so speed limits and separation distances must account for the robot’s stopping behavior. Safety-rated monitored stop can provide controlled braking with lower deceleration, whereas emergency stop is reserved for emergency or failure situations because abrupt braking may drop objects held by the robot. The cited work by Henriksson developed an algorithm for defining trajectory speed limits that prevent the robot from exceeding a virtual fence while stopping. The historical VTT system measured robot position using limit switches and detected humans with tactile mats; it used PLCs, relays, and the robot controller, but this is not evidence of current measurement practice. The excerpt mentions robot position and speed monitoring, cameras, sensor fusion, and simulated trajectory prediction in related safety systems, but it does not identify encoders, laser trackers, or high-speed cameras as instruments for experimentally measuring stopping distance.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide numerical stopping times or stopping distances for specific collaborative robots such as the UR10, UR5, or Franka Emika, nor does it describe a standardized braking-distance measurement procedure using encoders, laser trackers, or high-speed cameras. It only explains the safety principle that a robot moving toward a person must be able to stop before collision, with delays, brake response time, and the person’s forward-reaching motion included in the separation-distance calculation. The described dynamic safety system reduces robot speed according to the worker’s predicted position and increases speed as separation distance grows. Its primary motion-detection system uses two Microsoft Kinects, a PC, and the robot controller; the secondary safety layer uses two laser scanners and an ABB SafeMove safety controller. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide stopping times or stopping distances for specific collaborative robots such as the UR10, UR5, or Franka Emika, nor does it report braking-distance measurements for those models. It does provide relevant methodological guidance for measuring robot motion during stopping tests. External tracking systems can independently verify the robot’s reported velocity and reveal discrepancies between internally reported and actual motion. One approach estimates speed from discrete external pose samples, analogous to an outside observer tracking the tool center point (TCP). A second approach analytically estimates TCP speed from known feed-forward control laws, joint-angle changes, and the TCP’s distance from the robot base. The excerpt warns that position noise of only a few millimeters can significantly distort velocity estimates of several hundred millimeters per second. Accuracy depends on sampling frequency, the number of samples used, smoothing, and the measurement-uncertainty model; more samples reduce noise but can delay detection of velocity changes and bias results. The cited tracking example uses a LADAR-based system to measure an operator path, while the discussion also considers monitoring robot-base and TCP positions. The passage does not specifically identify encoders, laser trackers, or high-speed cameras as required instruments, although it supports combining robot-reported data with independently measured external position and velocity data.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents a six-level progressive autonomy framework for self-driving laboratories, ranging from Level 0 (manual operation) to Level 5 (full autonomy). Lower levels retain direct human control or require approval for each action. Level 2 allows AI execution under continuous human monitoring, while Level 3 permits unattended or largely autonomous operation only within strictly defined operational design domains (ODDs), with a human available on standby. Level 4 supports extended autonomous operation with periodic human oversight. Level 5 is described as theoretical and currently unattainable because of present AI limitations and regulatory constraints. Advancement between levels should depend on demonstrated competence, including typically hundreds of incident-free operations, rather than arbitrary schedules. Safety incidents or constraint violations trigger automatic regression to a lower autonomy level, and advancement requires root-cause analysis and verification of corrective action. The excerpt also emphasizes transparent plans, explicit safety assessments, anomaly-focused interfaces, and avoiding operator information overload. It discusses simulation, uncertainty quantification, formal verification of safety-critical software, and monitoring divergence between digital-twin predictions and physical observations. However, it does not provide specific rules for attended versus unattended operation, monitoring cameras, remote kill switches, or incident reports from robotic laboratories.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to developing safety tiers and operational safeguards for autonomous self-driving laboratories (SDLs), but it does not specify explicit attended-versus-unattended operating rules, requirements for monitoring cameras, or a remote kill-switch standard. It proposes classifying SDL safety levels using three factors: the system’s autonomy, the likelihood of accidents, and accident severity. Autonomy affects the scale and type of potential harm: collaborative spaces may increase human-injury risk, while highly autonomous systems may create greater property damage because they can conduct larger experiments. Risk also depends on the materials handled and the effectiveness of autonomous systems, while severity includes impacts on people, assets, and the environment. The authors advocate a dynamic, community-developed risk matrix modeled in part on biosafety levels. For operations, personnel should receive specialized training for human-robot shared spaces, safe maintenance, emergency procedures, and safety-rated monitored stops. The excerpt also supports retaining detailed operational data, decision-making records, environmental parameters, and AI/ML logs, analogous to aviation black boxes, to enable post-incident analysis. Governing bodies could define protocols, certify compliance, investigate accidents, and update procedures. Digital twins are presented as potential tools for safety analysis, risk prediction, training, and emergency-response practice.

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes human accountability and oversight rather than defining formal safety levels, tiers, or explicit attended-versus-unattended operating rules. It recommends that knowledgeable humans review and approve every experimental plan and executable code before an autonomous experiment runs. The review should address chemical and biological hazards, spill detection and containment, safe shutdown, material handling, mixing, disposal, and other project-specific risks. After approval, SDL systems should be compartmentalized so that plans and code cannot be altered. For security and operational monitoring, SDL operators should deploy systems capable of detecting unauthorized access, unexpected production or release of hazardous materials, and other consequential incidents. A human supervisor should remain available and empowered to pause or terminate an experiment, including through a “kill switch,” when malicious behavior or concealment, falsification, or obfuscation by the AI is detected. Such events should be reported to relevant authorities. The passage does not specifically require monitoring cameras, describe graded safety tiers, or provide empirical incident reports from robot-equipped laboratories. It notes that remote cloud laboratories are harder to observe directly, making timely intervention less likely, and that commercial cloud labs may provide additional screening, monitoring, and control protections.

contexts.context: The excerpt is only indirectly relevant to unattended-operation safety and does not specify formal safety levels, attended-versus-unattended operating rules, autonomy tiers, monitoring-camera requirements, remote kill-switch procedures, or incident-reporting data from laboratories using robots. It focuses instead on broader methods for validating and improving safety in self-driving laboratories. The authors identify the difficulty of predicting rare safety-critical events because most experiments proceed without incident, producing sparse safety data. They suggest using generative models and digital safety databases to create diverse synthetic hazardous scenarios and improve safety prediction and risk-management models. The excerpt also proposes digital twins—virtual replicas of physical laboratories updated with real-world data—as a way to test hypothetical or potentially catastrophic scenarios without conducting unsafe physical experiments. Physics-based simulation environments could reveal unknown constraints, benchmark robustness, and support experimental planning. In addition, virtual laboratories may provide immersive, risk-free training for personnel to practice routine operations, decision-making, and emergency responses. These points could inform the development of safety validation, simulation, and training frameworks for autonomous labs, but the excerpt provides no concrete operational policy or documented incident examples.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses unattended or extended autonomous SDL operation as a distinct safety and security challenge. Unlike conventional laboratories, an SDL may control experiments for weeks at a time, requiring mechanisms to supervise and contain machines handling hazardous materials or their precursors. The authors distinguish safety, involving unintentional harms such as toxic emissions, fires, explosions, or biological release, from security, involving intentional misuse or altered experimental objectives. Chemical and materials experiments generally involve small reagent quantities, which may limit the scale of incidents, whereas biological agents can self-replicate, so small initial quantities do not necessarily limit the impact of a release. The text notes that traditional laboratory safety depends on trained researchers, safety officers, regulations, and human responsibility, but SDLs disrupt this model. It recommends that future SDLs actively incorporate relevant chemical and biological safety information into their workflows and have AI systems operationalize that information for each experiment. However, this excerpt does not specify formal safety tiers, attended-versus-unattended operating rules, monitoring-camera requirements, remote emergency kill switches, or incident reports from robot-equipped laboratories.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial guidance relevant to SDL safety during attended and potentially unattended operation, but it does not define formal safety levels, tiers, camera requirements, or a remote kill-switch standard. It emphasizes that robotic systems reduce human exposure to hazardous substances while still requiring skilled personnel to monitor experiments, respond to malfunctions, and intervene in emergencies. Recommended robotic safeguards include a single point of control, reduced-speed modes, accessible emergency stops, collision detection, safety stops triggered by unexpected torque, and behavior that remains safe during power loss and restoration. For autonomous operation, ORGANA illustrates a human-in-the-loop model: anomalies trigger user disambiguation and troubleshooting rather than allowing the system to proceed without oversight. Its reporting capabilities could support safety documentation by incorporating SOPs, chemical SDS information, safety metrics, reported violations, and near-miss records. The excerpt also describes RABIT, which combines general and setup-specific rules, monitors command sequences for unmet preconditions, and enforces those rules through simulation, low-fidelity testing, and production environments. These mechanisms are relevant to defining operational controls and escalation procedures for unattended labs, but the provided pages do not report specific laboratory incidents involving robots or establish explicit attended-versus-unattended rules.

It recommends that orchestration platforms provide continuous real-time monitoring and alerts, including visibility into running experiments, device states, and failures requiring human intervention. The systems should implement automatic error handling and predefined protective responses, such as stopping pumps when pressure fluctuations suggest explosion risk, quenching exothermic reactions when temperatures exceed safe limits, and warning personnel not to enter when toxic gases are detected. For severe incidents, automatic contact with campus security, ambulance services, or fire departments is suggested, along with summaries of active experiments, hazards, and recommended actions for responders. The passage does not specifically mention monitoring cameras or a remote kill switch, although its discussion of monitoring, alerts, shutdown behavior, and emergency response is conceptually relevant to those mechanisms. It also reports no specific incident reports from laboratories operating robots. Before execution, SDL software should validate protocol integrity, parameter values, chemical safety compliance, and adherence to SOPs, potentially using simulations or dummy experiments. Existing platforms are described as using databases, dashboards, basic recovery routines, and parameter checks.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not define formal SDL safety levels, safety tiers, attended-versus-unattended operating rules, monitoring-camera requirements, or a remote kill-switch specification. It does, however, provide evidence relevant to establishing such safeguards. The RABIT framework combines general and setup-specific rules, monitors command sequences for unmet preconditions, and tests enforcement through simulation, low-fidelity test beds, and production environments. The authors emphasize that these controls cannot eliminate accidents, making personnel training and adherence to safety procedures essential when humans work with robots. Cited industrial evidence identifies inadequate safeguarding and insufficient warnings as leading causes of robot injuries, while other studies report that injuries may rise during the first two years of robotics adoption. Non-routine activities—including troubleshooting, maintenance, repair, inspection, and cleaning—are highlighted as especially vulnerable, with troubleshooting associated with many accidents. For unattended or remotely operated SDLs, the excerpt stresses cybersecurity and operational monitoring: internet connectivity can expose instruments to attacks, and compromised systems may have instruments tampered with, files stolen, protocols manipulated, or built-in safety measures overwritten, potentially harming nearby personnel. Recommended protections include collaboration with cybersecurity experts, encryption, IP whitelisting, multi-factor authentication, secure remote data storage, and stringent monitoring to prevent unauthorized remote access or control. These points could inform incident-reporting and escalation requirements, but no specific reporting format is given.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context. We run a small university cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, no joint brakes, no certified safety functions; it sags when power is removed), driven over CAN from a Raspberry Pi, with its supply switched by an IoT relay and a magnetic-switch E-stop on the supply. Our current state: the E-stop has never been tested; rebooting the controlling Pi cuts the arm's power mid-move and the arm drops; a hazard analysis and SOP are drafted but not reviewed; unattended runs are not allowed yet; the arm shares an enclosure with Raspberry Pi cameras and will tend consumer 3D printers and move vials, SEM stubs and sealed powder jars near people. An earlier literature answer already covered safety architecture (hardwired dual-channel E-stops that bypass software, safe states versus de-energizing, retry policies, no unattended combustible metal powder). We now need the verification side: how to test and document that what we built actually works, at university-lab cost.

Question.
(1) Test procedures and acceptance criteria for emergency-stop and protective-stop functions on small robot arms: what IEC 60204-1 (stop categories 0, 1, 2), ISO 13850, ISO 13849-2 (validation) and ISO 10218-1/-2:2025 require or recommend; how stopping time and stopping distance are measured (instruments, number of repetitions, worst-case pose and payload); and published examples of such tests on cobots or low-cost arms.
(2) Arms without brakes: published measurements or analyses of what happens on power loss (drop distance and speed under gravity, by pose and payload), and mitigations used on low-cost or hobby arms (mechanical brakes, back-drive resistance, controlled-stop before de-energizing, rest poses, UPS-backed controllers, supported park positions).
(3) Collision testing with inexpensive instruments: measuring transient and quasi-static contact force and pressure against ISO/TS 15066 body-region limits using force gauges, load cells, pressure-sensitive film or low-cost biofidelic pads, with reported accuracy versus commercial collision-measurement devices; and measured collision forces for low-cost arms (PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, myCobot, xArm Lite, UFactory or similar) if any exist.
(4) Risk assessment and documentation for robots in academic research labs: what university EHS programs (published policies, guidance documents or papers) require before a robot cell runs, including attended versus unattended operation, training, signage, interlocks, and periodic re-verification; and any incident reports involving low-cost or educational robot arms.
(5) A minimal, defensible verification plan for a cell like ours: which tests to run first, with how many repetitions, and what records to keep.

Prefer peer-reviewed sources and published standards or official guidance from 2010 to 2026; flag preprints, theses and vendor documents. For each claim give the DOI, standard clause or URL and quote the supporting sentence. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


# Verification Testing and Documentation for a Low-Cost Robot Arm in a University Cloud Lab

## 1. Emergency-Stop and Protective-Stop Test Procedures and Acceptance Criteria

### 1.1 Stop Categories per IEC 60204-1

IEC 60204-1 defines three stop categories that govern how robot motion ceases. Stop Category 0 is an uncontrolled stop: "power is removed from the actuators" immediately, prioritizing the fastest cessation without controlling the deceleration trajectory (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 3-3). Stop Category 1 is a controlled stop: "actuator power is maintained while the robot decelerates to a complete stop, after which power is removed and brakes are applied" (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 3-3). Stop Category 2 is a controlled stop where "actuator power remains available and the brakes are not applied after stopping" (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 3-3). The following table summarizes these categories and their implications for the PiPER arm:

| Stop Category | IEC 60204-1 Definition | Motor Power | Brakes Applied | ISO 13850 / ISO 10218 Use | Behavior on Brakeless Arm (PiPER) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | Uncontrolled stop by immediate removal of power to the machine actuators; the resulting trajectory is not controlled. (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 3-3) | Removed immediately | Applied if fitted; PiPER has none | ISO 13850 permits category 0 or 1 for emergency stop, selected by risk assessment. ISO 10218 permits category 0 for protective stops and requires category 0 if a controlled deceleration fails or unintended motion occurs. (jocelyn2019collaborativeroboticsassessment pages 45-47) | Torque disappears immediately; gravity can back-drive loaded joints, so the arm may sag or drop. “Power off” is therefore not necessarily a mechanically safe state. Measure both pre-de-energization stopping travel and subsequent gravity-driven displacement. |
| **1** | Controlled stop with actuator power maintained during deceleration; power is removed after standstill and brakes are then applied. (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 3-3) | Maintained while stopping, then removed | Applied after standstill if fitted; none on PiPER | ISO 13850 permits category 1 emergency stop where controlled stopping reduces risk. ISO 10218 permits category 1 protective stops. (jocelyn2019collaborativeroboticsassessment pages 45-47) | Can stop the commanded motion smoothly, but after power removal the unbraked arm can still sag or fall. It is acceptable only if the arm reaches a supported or gravity-stable pose before de-energization, or another holding measure prevents descent. |
| **2** | Controlled stop with actuator power remaining available after standstill; brakes are not applied. (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 3-3) | Remains energized | Not applied | Not an emergency-stop category under ISO 13850. ISO 10218 can permit category 2 as a protective stop where continued energized holding is justified and monitored. (jocelyn2019collaborativeroboticsassessment pages 45-47) | Active torque can hold pose and avoid gravity drop, but safety depends on the controller, drives, communications, and supply remaining functional. It is unsuitable as the sole response to Pi reboot, supply loss, or emergency isolation and requires restart prevention plus monitored standstill. |


*Table: IEC 60204-1 stop categories mapped to ISO 13850/ISO 10218 usage and the gravity-drop consequences of PiPER’s brakeless joints. The table distinguishes stopping commanded motion from maintaining a safe state afterward.*

### 1.2 ISO 13850, ISO 10218, and ISO 13849-2 Requirements

ISO 13850 permits either Category 0 or Category 1 for emergency stops, selected on the basis of risk assessment. ISO 10218-1:2011 requires that in collaborative mode 1 (safety-rated monitored stop), any unintended motion or failure of braking deceleration must produce a Category 0 stop; in modes 2–4, violations of speed or position limits must produce a protective stop of at least Category 0 or Category 1 (jocelyn2019collaborativeroboticsassessment pages 45-47). The emergency-stop function should meet at least Performance Level d (PLd) with Category 3 architecture under ISO 13849-1 (jocelyn2019collaborativeroboticsassessment pages 45-47). ISO 13849-2 provides validation procedures including fault exclusion analysis for different component technologies; the VTT guidelines note that "fault exclusions presented in ISO 13849-2 for different" technology types should be evaluated during cell verification (malm2017guidelinestomakeb pages 10-14).

### 1.3 Measuring Stopping Time and Distance

ISO 10218-1 Annex B provides provisions for evaluating stopping time (T_S) and braking distance (B), which "should be obtained through traceable measurements tied to the robot system under test" (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 5-7). These are not fixed constants: they vary with the robot's initial velocity, payload, pose, brake wear, and configuration (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 7-7). Marvel and Norcross describe a practical approach: trigger the safety system with a controlled event (e.g., a laser beam interrupted by the robot), run the robot along a repeatable trajectory, record its stop position, and repeat at multiple speeds (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 7-7). External tracking systems can independently verify the robot's reported velocity; however, position noise of only a few millimeters can significantly distort velocity estimates (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 5-5). For industrial robots, earlier systems at ~3 m/s had emergency-stop distances of approximately 40 cm and servo-stop distances of ~90 cm; a current ABB IRB 4600 at 2500 mm/s reportedly has a 65 cm servo-stop distance (malm2019dynamicsafetysystem pages 1-2).

### 1.4 Number of Repetitions

The CEN/CENELEC COVR guidelines for safety testing procedures in human-robot collaboration specify that "each test case is to be run at least three times" (normalisation2022guidelinesforthe pages 31-35). The COVR protocol specifies using "an accurate distance-measuring device, such as a laser meter with an error below 5%" or alternatively "another distance sensor or a motion-tracking system" (normalisation2022guidelinesforthe pages 31-35). Zimmermann et al. used 5 repetitions per pendulum test setting and 30 repetitions for one representative condition to establish repeatability, finding that maximum-force standard deviation was below 1% at 30 trials (zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 11-14).

### 1.5 Published Examples on Cobots

Jocelyn et al. assessed three collaborative robots and found that robots 1 and 2 generated Category 0 protective stops for modes 2–4, while robot 3 could generate Category 0 or 1 depending on configuration (jocelyn2019collaborativeroboticsassessment pages 45-47). Svarny et al. tested emergency stop on a UR10e (Stop 0) and KUKA iiwa (Stop 1) in the context of collision testing with protective soft skins. Mariano et al. tested UR5e and UR10e end-effectors in a self-driving laboratory, performing "repeated measurements...under the most restrictive manufacturer settings" to verify safety function response (mariano2026roboticsafetyin pages 7-8). **No published stop-test data exist for the AgileX PiPER or similar sub-$3k hobby-class arms.**

## 2. Arms Without Brakes: Power-Loss Behavior and Mitigations

### 2.1 The Fail-Passive Problem

For back-drivable arms without mechanical brakes, de-energizing does not automatically produce a safe state. Ding et al. formalize this as the "fail-passive gap": for a system whose safe condition requires active control (or at minimum gravitational stability), "classical Stop Category 0 power removal is not automatically safe" because gravity can back-drive the joints (ding2608towardcertifiedfunctional pages 1-2). Back-drivable actuators permit "forces applied at the arm output to move the actuator input," and the degree of back-drivability depends on gear ratio, friction, and motor cogging (ninhuijs2013overviewofactuated pages 4-6). Non-back-drivable mechanisms such as lead screws inherently resist passive movement but are uncommon on low-cost arms designed for compliance and safety during contact (ninhuijs2013overviewofactuated pages 4-6).

### 2.2 Published Measurements

**No published quantitative measurements of drop distance, descent speed, or settling behavior for the PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, myCobot, or similar low-cost brakeless arms were found in the peer-reviewed literature.** This is a significant gap. The closest analogue is cable-driven robot work by Fanton et al., who showed that "merely holding a pose normally requires continued motor input specifically to prevent cable backdriving" (fanton2016robustandefficient pages 1-2). For the PiPER, which uses servo motors with harmonic or planetary reducers, the back-drive resistance depends on the specific reducer's efficiency and friction coefficient, which is typically not published for hobby-grade actuators.

### 2.3 Mitigations

Several mitigation strategies are described in the literature:

- **Mechanical brakes:** Fanton et al. developed a Bi-Directional Self-Locking Clutch (BDSLC) that "requires no input power" and allows "motors can be shut down while the robot remains secured" (fanton2016robustandefficient pages 1-2). Electromagnetic brakes with fail-safe features that "maintain actuator position during power failures or system faults" are described by Ullah et al. (ullah2024linearactuatorusing pages 53-57).
- **Controlled stop before de-energizing (Category 1 approach):** The arm commands a gravity-stable or supported park pose before power removal, as the IEC 60204-1 Category 1 concept envisions: controlled deceleration followed by power removal (marvel2017implementingspeedand pages 3-3). For brakeless arms, the park pose must be one where gravity produces minimal or no torque on any joint, or where the arm rests on a physical support.
- **Rest/park poses:** Commanding the arm to a folded, gravity-stable configuration before de-energizing is a practical mitigation for the PiPER. The worst case for gravity drop is the fully extended horizontal pose.
- **UPS-backed controllers:** Not specifically discussed in the retrieved literature for small arms, but conceptually straightforward: a UPS on the controller and motor supply provides time for a Category 1 controlled stop sequence before supply exhaustion.
- **Physical supports/cradles:** A mechanical cradle at the park position catches the arm if it sags after de-energizing. This is analogous to the "supported park positions" concept and addresses the fundamental problem that brakeless arms cannot hold arbitrary poses unpowered.

### 2.4 First-Principles Analysis

For a 6-DOF arm with 500 mm reach and 1.5 kg payload held horizontally, a simple worst-case free-fall estimate gives: at the TCP, gravitational acceleration of ~9.8 m/s² produces ~70 mm of drop in the first 120 ms. However, actual behavior will be significantly slower due to motor cogging torque, gear-train friction, and viscous damping in the actuators. **This must be measured empirically for the specific PiPER arm** because the dominant terms—reducer back-drive friction and motor electromagnetic braking—are not publicly specified.

## 3. Collision Testing with Inexpensive Instruments

### 3.1 ISO/TS 15066 Body-Region Limits

ISO/TS 15066:2016 specifies biomechanical force and pressure limits for 29 body locations within 12 body regions. These limits originate from pain-onset studies using approximately 100 test subjects who generated about 9,000 analyzable measurements (ponikelsky2024forceandpressure pages 2-3). Quasi-static force and pressure limits are specified directly; transient-impact thresholds "can generally be calculated by multiplying the corresponding values by two" (scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 2-3). For example, the transient force limit for the back of the hand (body location 25) is 280 N (scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 6-8).

### 3.2 Commercial Biofidelic Devices

The standard measurement approach uses "biofidelic, biomechanically humanlike instruments and sensors with body-like features" (scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 2-3). Commercial devices such as the GTE CBSF-75 and CoboSafe include interchangeable spring constants (e.g., 75 N/mm for hand, 25 N/mm for sternum, 10 N/mm for abdomen) and damping elements (Shore hardness SH70 or SH10) to simulate different body regions (scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 3-5). Force sensors operate at ≥1 kHz, with signals filtered using a 100 Hz Butterworth low-pass filter (zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 5-7). Pressure measurement is typically via Fujifilm Prescale films, which are scanned, calibrated, and evaluated in software (ponikelsky2024forceandpressure pages 3-6).

### 3.3 Interlaboratory Variability

Scibilia et al. conducted an interlaboratory comparison across four European research centers (CNR, Fraunhofer IFF, DTI, CEA), performing 1,456 total tests on UR10/UR10e robots. Force generally increased linearly with velocity but included a nonzero force offset, deviating from the simple inelastic model predicted by ISO/TS 15066. Results were influenced by the robot controller, sensor fixture, and distance from the robot base (scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 5-6). Pressure measurements were found "difficult for end users to reproduce reliably because small robot or alignment differences and the cylindrical tool's edges generated high local pressure" (scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 6-8).

Zimmermann et al. compared three commercial biofidelic devices and found average peak-force differences of approximately 5% under identical conditions, with differences reaching up to 10% under matched bench conditions. Using 30 repeated measurements at one condition, peak-force standard deviation was below 1% (zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 11-14). The five-trial average standard deviations across the three devices were 1.4%, 0.4%, and 0.6% respectively (zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 11-14).

### 3.4 Low-Cost Alternatives

The following table compares available measurement approaches:

| Approach | Example Devices/Studies | Cost Range | Force Accuracy/Repeatability | Pressure Capability | Limitations | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Commercial biofidelic pressure-and-force measurement device (PFMD) | GTE Kolrobot 300N, GTE CBSF-75 Basic and CoboSafe; interchangeable springs and damping elements simulate body-region mechanics | Exact prices not reported; highest-cost option in this comparison | Three commercial devices differed by about 5% on average in a robot pre-study and by up to 10% under matched bench conditions. Five-trial average SD was 0.4–1.4%; one 30-trial condition had peak-force SD below 1%. | Yes, typically by separate pressure film or compatible pressure sensor; CoboSafe uses scanned and calibrated Fujifilm Prescale film | Results depend on spring rate, damping, moving mass, fixture stiffness, geometry, alignment and filtering; commercial-device agreement does not itself establish traceable accuracy | (zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 1-2, ponikelsky2024forceandpressure pages 3-6, scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 3-5, zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 11-14, zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 5-7) |
| Low-cost load cell plus spring/damper pad | Calibrated load cell or force gauge mounted behind a body-region-specific elastomer and mechanical spring; research analogue of the mass–spring–damper PFMD | Exact prices not reported; potentially low to moderate, depending on load cell, amplifier and data acquisition | No general accuracy figure was published for a DIY assembly. Commercial comparisons show that even nominally similar compliant devices can differ by 5–10%, so calibration of the complete assembled system is necessary; sampling of at least 1 kHz and documented filtering are appropriate benchmarks | No intrinsic pressure measurement; add calibrated pressure film or a pressure array | A bare load cell is not biofidelic. Compliance, damping, moving mass, bandwidth, fixture rigidity and dynamic calibration must be characterized; suitable for screening unless validated against a reference PFMD | (hartmann2026designvalidationand pages 1-2, zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 1-2, samarathunga2023considerationsonthe pages 2-3, zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 11-14, zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 5-7) |

A critical finding from Hartmann et al.'s systematic review is that "low-cost resistive sensors" lost signal linearity completely above approximately 150 N, with "correlation to a certified reference load cell collapsing because of uncompensated dynamic effects" (hartmann2026designvalidationand pages 54-55). This means inexpensive force-sensing resistors are unsuitable for validating compliance with ISO/TS 15066 transient limits, which often exceed 150 N.

A more defensible low-cost approach is a calibrated piezoelectric or strain-gauge load cell (≥1 kHz sampling) mounted behind a body-region-appropriate spring and elastomer pad, with Fuji Prescale film for pressure. This replicates the architecture of commercial PFMDs. However, ISO/TS 15066 "does not precisely define the measurement setup or measurement uncertainties," so "different instruments can produce different results under identical loads" (zimmermann2022experimentalcomparisonof pages 1-2).

### 3.5 Measured Collision Forces for Low-Cost Arms

**No published collision-force measurements were found for the AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, myCobot, or other sub-$3k arms.** For the UR10 at speeds up to 400 mm/s, Ponikelský et al. measured forces up to 446 N near the robot base (ponikelsky2024forceandpressure pages 3-6). For the BYU PiPER with its 1.5 kg payload and lower mass, collision forces are expected to be substantially lower due to the smaller effective mass. The arm's low mass (likely <5 kg total moving mass) may place most operating configurations well below ISO/TS 15066 transient limits even at moderate speeds, but this must be verified empirically.

## 4. Risk Assessment and Documentation for Robots in Academic Research Labs

### 4.1 Applicable Standards Framework

Robot cells in academic laboratories are subject to the same fundamental safety standards as industrial installations. ISO 12100 provides the general risk-assessment process; ISO 10218-1 and ISO 10218-2 address robot and robot-system safety respectively (the latter is "particularly directed to system integrators"); ISO/TS 15066 provides collaborative-robot-specific guidance; and ANSI/RIA R15.06-2012 addresses "safe design, installation, operation, risk assessment, safety systems, training, and maintenance" (ertekin2024interdisciplinaryseniordesign pages 3-5, malm2017guidelinestomakea pages 10-14). The integrator—which in a university lab is typically the research group—assumes responsibility for the completed cell because it incorporates guarding, protective devices, and other equipment (malm2017guidelinestomakeb pages 10-14).

### 4.2 Self-Driving Laboratory Safety

Mariano et al. present the most directly relevant published framework for robot safety in self-driving/cloud laboratories. Their methodology uses an iterative six-step process: "define the system, identify hazards, analyze scenarios, estimate risk, reduce risk, and validate the resulting safeguards" (mariano2026roboticsafetyin pages 1-2). In their Swiss case study (CAT+ West Hub), sixteen hazards were identified; robot–human collisions and chemical exposure were considered most critical. They emphasize that "collaborative robots should not be presumed safe and require rigorous validation, including experimental force and pressure measurements under realistic operating conditions" (mariano2026roboticsafetyin pages 1-2). Safety laser scanners were validated to detect personnel and trigger an immediate stop, and "safety-zone dimensions were checked against minimum separation distances in ISO 13857:2020" (mariano2026roboticsafetyin pages 8-9). **This is a peer-reviewed paper** (SLAS Technology, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.slast.2026.100463).

### 4.3 Attended vs. Unattended Operation

Zhang et al. propose a six-level autonomy framework for SDLs: Level 0 (manual) through Level 5 (full autonomy). Level 2 allows "AI execution under continuous human monitoring," while Level 3 permits "unattended or largely autonomous operation only within strictly defined operational design domains (ODDs), with a human available on standby." Advancement requires "typically hundreds of incident-free operations" rather than arbitrary schedules, and safety incidents trigger "automatic regression to a lower autonomy level" (zhang2026safesdlestablishingsafetyboundaries pages 9-11). **This is a preprint** (arXiv, Feb 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2602.15061).

Tobias and Wahab recommend that "knowledgeable humans review and approve every experimental plan and executable code before an autonomous experiment runs" and that "a human supervisor should remain available and empowered to pause or terminate an experiment, including through a 'kill switch'" (tobias2025autonomousselfdrivinglaboratoriesa pages 17-18).

Leong et al. recommend that "personnel should receive specialized training for human-robot shared spaces, safe maintenance, emergency procedures, and safety-rated monitored stops" and advocate retaining "detailed operational data, decision-making records, environmental parameters, and AI/ML logs, analogous to aviation black boxes, to enable post-incident analysis" (leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 26-30). **This is a preprint** (ChemRxiv, Dec 2024; DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-2qx28).

### 4.4 Training and Signage

ANSI/RIA R15.06-2012 requires that the risk assessment identify hazards, estimate likelihood and severity, and determine protective measures. Training should include "robot programming, troubleshooting, and emergency-response procedures." Safeguards should include "emergency-stop buttons, safety interlocks, and protective barriers" (ertekin2024interdisciplinaryseniordesign pages 3-5). The VTT guidelines specify that the risk assessment should establish "intended use, operating modes, training, exposure, space and time limits, environmental conditions, and other relevant constraints" (malm2017guidelinestomakea pages 22-27).

### 4.5 Incident Reports

**No published incident reports specifically involving low-cost or educational robot arms in university laboratories were found in the peer-reviewed literature.** Leong et al. cite industrial evidence that "inadequate safeguarding and insufficient warnings" are leading causes of robot injuries, and that "injuries may rise during the first two years of robotics adoption." Non-routine activities—"including troubleshooting, maintenance, repair, inspection, and cleaning—are highlighted as especially vulnerable" (leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 13-16). **University-specific EHS policies for robot arms are largely unpublished internal documents;** no peer-reviewed compilation was found.

### 4.6 Periodic Re-Verification

No single cited standard mandates a fixed re-verification interval. The general principle from ISO 12100 and related standards is that "risk assessment and validation should be repeated after mitigation and when tasks, environment or operators change; ongoing monitoring should include close calls, incidents and feedback" (belzile2022safetyfirston pages 7-10, malm2017guidelinestomakea pages 22-27). Zhang et al. recommend re-verification "after incidents, constraint violations, corrective changes, or evidence of model or sensor degradation" rather than on a fixed calendar (zhang2026safesdlestablishingsafetyboundaries pages 9-11).

### 5.1 Recommended Test Sequence

**Phase 1 (Before any operation near people):**
1. **V-01: E-stop functional test.** Verify the magnetic-switch E-stop actually removes power independently of software. This has never been tested. Use a multimeter or oscilloscope to confirm supply drops to zero within milliseconds of actuation. Test at minimum 3 times per condition (empty and loaded, multiple poses) (normalisation2022guidelinesforthe pages 31-35).
2. **V-02: Gravity-drop characterization.** With the E-stop confirmed working, deliberately cut power in multiple poses and payloads and measure the resulting sag with calibrated video. This characterizes the actual hazard envelope.
3. **V-03: Controlled park test.** Implement and test a software-commanded park-to-supported-pose routine that completes before the IoT relay opens.
4. **V-04: Pi reboot test.** Deliberately reboot the Pi during motion and verify the arm does not produce hazardous motion on restart.

**Phase 2 (Before attended operation near people):**
5. **V-05: Collision force screening.** Using a calibrated load cell behind appropriate padding, measure peak contact forces at the worst-case pose and speed. Even screening data provides a defensible basis for speed limits.
6. **V-07: SOP walkthrough and training.** Every authorized user must complete training including emergency-stop actuation, spill response, and energy isolation.

**Phase 3 (Before considering unattended operation):**
7. **V-06: Perimeter safeguarding test** (if safety scanners or interlocks are added).
8. **V-08: Establish periodic re-verification schedule.**

### 5.2 Records

For each test, the minimum defensible record should include: test protocol with acceptance criteria defined before testing; date and personnel; hardware/software configuration and versions; raw data (video, traces, logs); results and comparison to acceptance criteria; anomalies and corrective actions; and reviewer signature (normalisation2022guidelinesforthea pages 7-10, malm2017guidelinestomakea pages 22-27). The VTT guidelines state that the responsible entity must "perform and document a risk assessment, address all applicable safety requirements and directives...compile and maintain a technical file" (malm2017guidelinestomakeb pages 10-14).

### 5.3 Key Gaps and Limitations

Several important limitations should be noted:

- **No published safety data exist for the PiPER arm or similar sub-$3k arms.** All stop-test, drop-test, and collision-force measurements must be generated locally. This is original characterization work, not verification against manufacturer specifications.
- **The PiPER's magnetic-switch E-stop on the supply line implements a de facto Stop Category 0,** but on a brakeless arm this may not achieve a mechanically safe state. A controlled-park-then-de-energize sequence (approximating Category 1) is strongly recommended as the normal shutdown path.
- **Low-cost resistive force sensors are unsuitable for ISO/TS 15066 validation** above approximately 150 N due to complete loss of linearity (hartmann2026designvalidationand pages 54-55). A calibrated strain-gauge or piezoelectric load cell at ≥1 kHz is the minimum defensible instrument.
- **University EHS robot-specific policies are largely unpublished.** The lab should work with BYU's EHS office to establish local requirements, using the ISO 12100 / ISO 10218-2 framework and the SDL safety literature as a basis.
- **Unattended operation should not be attempted until Phase 1 and Phase 2 are complete,** all results are documented and reviewed, and the risk assessment explicitly addresses unattended failure modes. The Safe-SDL framework suggests requiring "hundreds of incident-free operations" before advancing autonomy levels (zhang2026safesdlestablishingsafetyboundaries pages 9-11).

This verification plan is designed to be achievable at university-lab cost using instruments likely available in an engineering department (oscilloscope, calibrated video, load cell, multimeter) while producing documentation that meets the intent of ISO 10218-2's verification requirements and the emerging SDL safety literature.

| Stop Category | IEC 60204-1 Definition | Motor Power | Brakes Applied | ISO 13850 / ISO 10218 Use | Behavior on Brakeless Arm (PiPER) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | Uncontrolled stop by immediate removal of power to the machine actuators; the resulting trajectory is not controlled. (pqac-00000001) | Removed immediately | Applied if fitted; PiPER has none | ISO 13850 permits category 0 or 1 for emergency stop, selected by risk assessment. ISO 10218 permits category 0 for protective stops and requires category 0 if a controlled deceleration fails or unintended motion occurs. (pqac-00000000) | Torque disappears immediately; gravity can back-drive loaded joints, so the arm may sag or drop. “Power off” is therefore not necessarily a mechanically safe state. Measure both pre-de-energization stopping travel and subsequent gravity-driven displacement. |
| **1** | Controlled stop with actuator power maintained during deceleration; power is removed after standstill and brakes are then applied. (pqac-00000001) | Maintained while stopping, then removed | Applied after standstill if fitted; none on PiPER | ISO 13850 permits category 1 emergency stop where controlled stopping reduces risk. ISO 10218 permits category 1 protective stops. (pqac-00000000) | Can stop the commanded motion smoothly, but after power removal the unbraked arm can still sag or fall. It is acceptable only if the arm reaches a supported or gravity-stable pose before de-energization, or another holding measure prevents descent. |
| **2** | Controlled stop with actuator power remaining available after standstill; brakes are not applied. (pqac-00000001) | Remains energized | Not applied | Not an emergency-stop category under ISO 13850. ISO 10218 can permit category 2 as a protective stop where continued energized holding is justified and monitored. (pqac-00000000) | Active torque can hold pose and avoid gravity drop, but safety depends on the controller, drives, communications, and supply remaining functional. It is unsuitable as the sole response to Pi reboot, supply loss, or emergency isolation and requires restart prevention plus monitored standstill. |


*Table: IEC 60204-1 stop categories mapped to ISO 13850/ISO 10218 usage and the gravity-drop consequences of PiPER’s brakeless joints. The table distinguishes stopping commanded motion from maintaining a safe state afterward.*

(pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045) | Every individual result plus measurement uncertainty remains below the applicable force and pressure limits. info.query:
Context. We run a small university cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, no joint brakes, no certified safety functions; it sags when power is removed), driven over CAN from a Raspberry Pi, with its supply switched by an IoT relay and a magnetic-switch E-stop on the supply. Our current state: the E-stop has never been tested; rebooting the controlling Pi cuts the arm's power mid-move and the arm drops; a hazard analysis and SOP are drafted but not reviewed; unattended runs are not allowed yet; the arm shares an enclosure with Raspberry Pi cameras and will tend consumer 3D printers and move vials, SEM stubs and sealed powder jars near people. An earlier literature answer already covered safety architecture (hardwired dual-channel E-stops that bypass software, safe states versus de-energizing, retry policies, no unattended combustible metal powder). We now need the verification side: how to test and document that what we built actually works, at university-lab cost.

Question.
(1) Test procedures and acceptance criteria for emergency-stop and protective-stop functions on small robot arms: what IEC 60204-1 (stop categories 0, 1, 2), ISO 13850, ISO 13849-2 (validation) and ISO 10218-1/-2:2025 require or recommend; how stopping time and stopping distance are measured (instruments, number of repetitions, worst-case pose and payload); and published examples of such tests on cobots or low-cost arms.
(2) Arms without brakes: published measurements or analyses of what happens on power loss (drop distance and speed under gravity, by pose and payload), and mitigations used on low-cost or hobby arms (mechanical brakes, back-drive resistance, controlled-stop before de-energizing, rest poses, UPS-backed controllers, supported park positions).
(3) Collision testing with inexpensive instruments: measuring transient and quasi-static contact force and pressure against ISO/TS 15066 body-region limits using force gauges, load cells, pressure-sensitive film or low-cost biofidelic pads, with reported accuracy versus commercial collision-measurement devices; and measured collision forces for low-cost arms (PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, myCobot, xArm Lite, UFactory or similar) if any exist.
(4) Risk assessment and documentation for robots in academic research labs: what university EHS programs (published policies, guidance documents or papers) require before a robot cell runs, including attended versus unattended operation, training, signage, interlocks, and periodic re-verification; and any incident reports involving low-cost or educational robot arms.
(5) A minimal, defensible verification plan for a cell like ours: which tests to run first, with how many repetitions, and what records to keep.

Prefer peer-reviewed sources and published standards or official guidance from 2010 to 2026; flag preprints, theses and vendor documents. For each claim give the DOI, standard clause or URL and quote the supporting sentence. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
